to be revealed through good works, for it is not a work of a sound mind to sometimes apostatize from divine laws and then again to take hold of them as if waking up from sleep, like those who fall from ships in the middle of the sea and waves, who, having escaped fear, neglect their safety, and when they are in evil, they see what is useful, and again, swimming back to the ship, they seek safety from where they fell, but rather one should not wait for the end of danger, but hate it before it comes, for thus they would counsel more soundly, and if it seems to everyone that imitating those who accept such things is full of foolishness, and they marvel at what is rightly censured, how should they not bring all eagerness to be possessed by divine laws and offer a blameless polity, and hear again what the divine law proclaims to us about these things, and the Lord spoke, saying, to command Aaron and his sons, this is the law of the whole burnt offering, which is to be on the altar all night until morning, and the fire of the altar will be burning on it, and will not be extinguished

Open your mouth and I will fill it; having been encouraged by the grace of our Savior, we have clarity in these matters. The philanthropic Word of God draws all to piety and stirs up to virtue those who think they should be obedient to His laws. Not all have the same zeal for this, nor is each one led by the same eagerness. Some approach God more diligently, considering nothing more important than devotion to Him, and offer themselves as a whole and undivided sacrifice to the Lord. This is truly a whole burnt offering, when someone offers themselves entirely to God, not working evil at any time. The law of whole burnt offering says that it should be on the altar all night until morning, and the fire on the altar should not be extinguished, which is the relationship with the Holy Spirit in us, as the Savior indicated, saying 'I came to cast fire on the earth'. The one being wholly burnt and offered entirely to God should keep the inextinguishable fire on themselves and always have the power of that holy flame in them, for the whole night, which is taken to mean the present life.

But then again the mind is to be rekindled, but there is to be a certain single way, and always zealous in spirit, as Paul says. But it would be clearer for us through other examples if we were to carefully examine the will of the law. For God says again in sequence to the high priest Moses: 'And these are the things that you will do on the altar. Two year-old lambs on the altar continually, a perpetual burnt offering. You will make one lamb in the morning and the second lamb in the evening, and a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil and a fourth of a hin of wine for the one lamb.' But there is also through these things for us to understand clearly that no time is to be allowed to pass without God being properly honored, receiving from us the fragrance of good works, as if some continuous sacrifice. For commanding one lamb to be slaughtered at the beginning of the day and the second at the end, it seems to signify all time, encompassing the middle through the extremes. And he wants the fine flour to be mixed with wine and oil, not commanding the full measure to be placed on it, but a fourth of a hin.

Through a certain riddle, teaching that those who continually offer honor to God, and as it were bring a sacrifice to the lawgiver with greater fervor, having been pitied, will rejoice, having received a small part of the gift in the present life, but in the future age, the fullness of grace will be given to them, when, as the prophet says, 'Eternal joy will be over their heads', and pain and sighing will flee, the law commands not to deviate from the right path, how will we not be liable for all punishment, having neglected such good things, if one considers human nature, it seems that the tone of such conduct is difficult, the law shows a way of life that is easier than what was said, and more attainable

For when God appeared to the sons of Israel in fire and darkness and storm, and established laws regarding deeds, Moses, thinking it necessary to show the sons of Israel the type of polity pleasing to the lawgiver through a clear deed, since they were not yet able to receive the perfect things, does something like this; saying that Moses rose early, built an altar under the mountain, and sent young men to offer whole burnt offerings and sacrifices of salvation to God; then Moses took half of the blood, poured it into a bowl, and poured the other half towards the altar; we know each of the written things, examining them carefully, what kind of benefit appears to us from this; Moses rises, builds an altar, teaching us that it is necessary to awaken as if from sleep, and for man to rise to sobriety, having passed through the cloud of sin like a dark night, and now running towards the light of knowledge; so that he may establish his own mind as a good altar to God; I think the prophet Isaiah also said this; 'My spirit rises from the night towards you, God, because your commandments are light on the earth'; this is what Moses' rising means

But in order to follow the sequence of the thought, we proceed to the arrangement of what is being sought. The altar is placed not on the mountain, but under the mountain, which indicates the humble mindset of those who are still lacking in perfection and are not yet able to ascend to the heights of perfect commandments, but are near to them. Nevertheless, they have approached God. Then, twelve stones are to be placed around the altar, corresponding to the twelve tribes of Israel. Through this, we learn that we ought to always be present with God, never falling into sinful behavior. The Psalmist declares this to us more clearly, saying: 'I will encircle your altar, Lord.' After this, he says again: 'He sent out the young men of the sons of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed a salvation sacrifice to God, calves.' It is not the task of the sluggish or weak-minded to offer sacrifices to God, but rather of the youthful and noble-minded. For this reason, the young men are said to have been sent, and they offer a salvation sacrifice, calves.
pass_b_english: It is through good works that one's true character is revealed. A sound mind would not lead someone to abandon divine laws at times, only to return to them later as if waking up from a sleep. This behavior is comparable to those who fall off a ship in the middle of the sea and are tossed about by waves. Having escaped the initial fear, they neglect their safety and only realize what is useful when they are in the midst of evil. Then, they try to swim back to the ship, seeking safety from the very place they fell.

One should not wait for the end of danger to arrive, but rather hate it before it comes. This approach would be more sound. If it seems to everyone that imitating those who accept such things is full of foolishness, and they marvel at what is rightly censured, then they should bring all eagerness to be guided by divine laws and offer a blameless way of life. And if anyone, seeing the foolishness of such a thing, accepts the imitation of those who do this, how should they not bring all eagerness to be possessed by divine laws and offer a blameless polity? Hear again what the divine law proclaims to us about these things: "And the Lord spoke, saying, 'Command Aaron and his sons: This is the law of the whole burnt offering. This is the whole burnt offering upon the altar, all night until morning, and the fire of the altar shall burn upon it, it shall not be extinguished'" (Leviticus 6:8-13).

As we have been encouraged by the grace of our Savior, we can approach God with confidence, and it is this confidence that allows us to understand the importance of devotion to Him. The Word of God, which is philanthropic in nature, draws all people to piety and encourages them to live virtuous lives, stirring up those who are obedient to His laws to strive for excellence. However, not everyone has the same level of enthusiasm for this, and each person is led by their own unique eagerness.

Some individuals are more diligent in their approach to God, considering nothing more important than their devotion to Him, and they offer themselves as a whole and undivided sacrifice to the Lord. This is what it means to be a whole burnt offering, where one offers themselves entirely to God, without any reservation or evil intent. The law of the whole burnt offering says: "This is the whole burnt offering, all night upon the altar until morning. And the fire of the altar shall burn upon it, it shall not be extinguished" (Leviticus 6:12-13). This fire can be seen as a symbol of the Holy Spirit's presence in us, which the Savior referred to when He said, "I came to cast fire on the earth" (Luke 12:49). The one who is wholly devoted to God should strive to keep this inextinguishable fire burning within them, always having the power of the holy flame in their life, for the whole night, which represents the present life.

The mind must be continually rekindled, and there should be a single, unwavering approach to spiritual life, always zealous in spirit, as Paul teaches. By examining the law carefully, we can gain a deeper understanding of God's will, and this is made clearer through various examples. For instance, God instructs the high priest Moses on the proper way to offer sacrifices on the altar.

The command to offer two year-old lambs on the altar every day, one in the morning and one in the evening, along with a specific amount of fine flour mixed with oil and wine, signifies the importance of continuous worship and honor to God. This ritual encompasses all time, from the beginning to the end of each day, and reminds us that no moment should pass without acknowledging and honoring God. The use of wine, oil, and fine flour in the offering also holds significance, as it represents the fragrance of good works that we are to offer to God continually, like a perpetual sacrifice. Through a certain riddle, teaching that those who continually offer honor to God, and as it were bring a sacrifice to the lawgiver with greater fervor, having been pitied, will rejoice, having received a small part of the gift in the present life, but in the future age, the fullness of grace will be given to them, when, as the prophet says, "Eternal joy will be over their heads, and pain and sighing will flee" (Isaiah 35:10). The law commands us not to deviate from the right path, and if we neglect such good things, we will be liable for all punishment.

If one considers human nature, it seems that the tone of such conduct is difficult, but the law shows a way of life that is easier than what was said, and more attainable. The law provides a solution to the problem of human weakness, and it is possible to follow it without being overwhelmed by its demands.

When God appeared to the sons of Israel in fire, darkness, and storm, and established laws regarding their actions, Moses, thinking it necessary to show them the type of polity pleasing to the lawgiver through a clear deed, did something remarkable. He rose early, built an altar under the mountain, and sent young men to offer whole burnt offerings and sacrifices of salvation to God. This act was a demonstration of the kind of benefit that appears to us from this event.

Moses' rising early and building an altar teaches us that it is necessary to awaken as if from sleep and rise to sobriety, having passed through the cloud of sin like a dark night, and now running towards the light of knowledge. By doing so, we establish our own mind as a good altar to God, a concept also expressed by the prophet Isaiah when he said, "My spirit rises from the night towards you, God, because your commandments are light on the earth" (Isaiah 26:9). This is the significance of Moses' rising early, a symbol of our own spiritual awakening and growth.

As we follow the sequence of thought, we proceed to the arrangement of what is being sought. The placement of the altar, not on the mountain but under it, signifies the humble mindset of those who are still lacking in perfection and are not yet able to ascend to the heights of perfect commandments, but are near to them. This indicates that they have approached God, albeit in a state of humility.

The presence of twelve stones around the altar, corresponding to the twelve tribes of Israel, teaches us that we ought to always be present with God, never falling into sinful behavior. The Psalmist declares this to us more clearly, saying: "I will encircle your altar, Lord" (Psalm 87:1). After this, he says again: "He sent out the young men of the sons of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed a salvation sacrifice to God, calves" (Leviticus 1:3). This emphasizes the importance of a youthful and noble-minded approach to offering sacrifices to God.

It is not the task of the sluggish or weak-minded to offer sacrifices to God, but rather of the youthful and noble-minded. For this reason, the young men are said to have been sent, and they offer a salvation sacrifice, calves. This highlights the significance of a strong and virtuous mindset in our relationship with God.
